    About this map

    What is counted: a calendar day counts when its 30-year average high (1991–2020) is above 70°F, or below 50°F. That is the length of the typical warm or cold season, the same idea WeatherSpark uses. It is not the number of actual days that hit those temperatures in a given year, which depends on the weather.

    The data: PRISM 1991–2020 climate normals. The 800-meter monthly mean and low temperatures set the level for every grid cell, and PRISM's 4-kilometer daily normals give the day-by-day shape. PRISM defines the mean as the average of high and low, so the average high is twice the mean minus the low. That matches PRISM's own published daily highs to within 0.001°F.

    The equal-days line traces where a place has as many days with average highs above 70°F as below 50°F. East of the Rockies it runs from eastern Wyoming across southern South Dakota and northern Iowa, just north of Chicago, along the Ohio–Michigan line and Lake Erie, across central Pennsylvania, and through Connecticut, passing just south of Boston. North of it, cold days outnumber warm days. In the West, elevation matters more than latitude: the line loops around mountain ranges (more cold days) and warm valleys, and small loops mark the high peaks of West Virginia and the Great Smokies.

    Season dates mark the longest unbroken stretch above 70°F or below 50°F.

    Sources: PRISM Climate Group, Oregon State University, 1991–2020 normals (800 m monthly, 4 km daily); US Census Bureau 2023 gazetteer and population estimates. Map projection: US Albers equal-area.
